# C# 14 extension export and declaration metadata qualification

This fixture qualifies the compiler portion of SF-A02-T83 / #664 that exports C# 14
extension blocks for independent Roslyn consumers. It also qualifies the shared
unmanaged, readonly-reference, scoped-reference and compiler-attribute metadata
used by ordinary declarations and their extension declaration copies.

This is a bounded interoperability checkpoint. It does not close all remaining
extension-language acceptance in #664.

## Metadata contract

The real implementation remains the original static `MethodDef` on its original
container. Public nested grouping declarations describe extension methods,
properties and operators; their skeleton bodies throw
`NotImplementedException`. Marker types and `ExtensionMarkerAttribute` connect the
metadata declarations to their source receiver. Roslyn clients are checked to call
the original implementations, including when compiled against the reference
assembly and then run with the implementation assembly.

Grouping keys normalize CLR signatures and constraints. Exact marker declarations
preserve receiver attributes, generic constraints and nullable annotations. Key
construction includes assembly identity, attribute constructor parameter types,
boxed constant types and floating-point bits, with explicit traversal limits.
Type keys stop at open generic definitions to avoid definition/parameter cycles.

Grouping constraint copies erase nullable and tuple transforms without mutating
source symbols. Their metadata plans suppress type-level annotation/context
emission; actual member entries and exact marker child scopes remain active.
The test compares both declaration orders with Roslyn and distinguishes absent
raw metadata from annotations inherited through an enclosing nullable context.

Property, getter, setter and static-only receiver attributes bind at their actual
declaration targets. The original lowered accessors keep their method identity.
A genuine static extension `Main` remains an entry-point candidate; only its
metadata-only grouping declaration is excluded from entry-point discovery.

Unmanaged constraints include their required custom modifier and marker.
Readonly/reference parameter and return metadata is shared with ordinary methods
and delegate `Invoke`, not special-cased to extension members. Missing compiler
attributes use the per-writer registry and its common constructor/body metadata.
The closed reference surface exercises this fallback; it is not an old-framework
qualification claim.

The original frozen qualification produced 15 passing and 19 failing tests out of

Two test harness assumptions were also corrected against real Roslyn output.
The dedicated entry-point repro confirmed that Roslyn accepts a static extension
`Main` and that SharpForge had incorrectly counted its metadata copy twice.

After those corrections, the first focused repeat passed 29/29 with zero skips.
The broader 16-file check at `bbd2384e` passed 109/110 with zero skips. Its single
failure was the adjacent nullable oracle's function-pointer signature, which this
isolated worktree had not yet imported from the qualified pointer workstream.
After applying that exact dependency, the three affected nullable/delegate/constraint
files passed 10/10 with zero skips at `ed910584`. This is an adjacent check followed
by a targeted dependency repeat, not a claim that one 110-test run passed at the
final head.

Native coverage includes implementation and reference assemblies, actual call

The existing preview indexer tests are adjacent source-VM/image-path checks;

`git diff --check` passed. The advisory structure checker exited zero while

### Final empty-scope equivalence check

The approved scope-pruning correction in `acd08247` then passed **35/35 tests with
zero skips** across its new control and six adjacent files. The actual
pre-optimization compiler at clean `ed910584` produced
[no-transform-metadata.json](no-transform-metadata.json), explicitly a SharpForge
byte-equivalence control rather than a Roslyn oracle.

The control preserves raw nullable attribute blobs, Param rows and GenericParam
numbers/flags/constraint annotations for 29 declarations on each of the closed
registry and actual .NET PE reference surfaces. Both assembly APIs match that
control. It covers initially empty methods, nonempty `[0]` generic and oblivious
context votes, return-only context `2`, nested generic declarations, and primitive
and generic delegates. A zero-length transform is distinguished from `[0]` before
context compression.

```sh
node scripts/limited.js node --test --test-concurrency=1 \
  tests/compiler-nullable-empty-method-scopes.test.js \
  tests/compiler-nullable-metadata.test.js \
  tests/compiler-nullable-metadata-flags.test.js \
  tests/compiler-nullable-delegate-signatures.test.js \
  tests/compiler-extension-constraint-normalization.test.js \
  tests/compiler-declaration-ref-metadata.test.js \
  tests/compiler-exported-extension-native.test.js
```

## Compilation benchmark

The measured operation is a complete `compileToReferenceAssembly` call using the
closed registry reference surface, C# 14 and fixed source text. This compares the
whole metadata composition, including nullable, tuple, common compiler attributes,
ref safety and the pointer signature dependency. It does not isolate hashing or
one metadata helper. Sources deliberately contain 32 members per workload; distinct
receiver names in the extension workloads require 32 exact marker declarations,
while equivalent CLR groups are shared.

Every accepted run records clean compiler revisions and the same source hashes.
The baseline is `b19a56a77080e63ba1a216c7944971e5ca00b27f`, immediately before the new
export/shared metadata composition. Initial captures use candidate
`ed91058416e8c1bbd40fdf3d778f07f615c410c8`; the final paired capture uses
`acd0824747762f358db9d81f4173e18177bb8d42`. The only production difference between
those candidates is omission of nullable method scopes that initially contain no
metadata entries. Nonempty vectors, including `[0]`, are retained.

Machine: Node v24.19.0, Linux x64, AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor. Captures ran
through `scripts/limited.js` and the team's serial slot. The host was shared, not
isolated. No resource-limit override or manual semaphore cleanup was used. These
measurements are observations, not confidence intervals or a portable performance
gate. Output sizes are identical across every capture of the corresponding side.

### Final same-process paired capture

Both complete compiler graphs are loaded into one Node process. Each graph and
workload receives 80 rotating warmups, followed by 20 samples of one compilation
each. Workload/side traversal reverses on odd warmup and sample rounds. GC is
requested before every measured compilation. The exact same paired harness was
used for the original and final comparisons; its SHA-256 is
`0e29a734fa90447e87e509d44387cff738b8ec30b2014035df72ae6976610476`.

```sh
node scripts/limited.js node --expose-gc scripts/benchmarks/a02-extension-metadata-paired.mjs \
  --baseline-entry /absolute/path/to/clean-baseline/packages/compiler/src/index.js \
  --candidate-entry /absolute/path/to/clean-candidate/packages/compiler/src/index.js \
  --members 32 --samples 20 > paired.json
```

Raw final capture: [benchmark-paired-final.json](benchmark-paired-final.json).

| Workload | Median before → after (ms) | Median change | p95 before → after (ms) | p95 change | PE bytes before → after | Size change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ordinary-methods | 11.420 → 11.333 | -0.77% | 14.610 → 15.065 | +3.11% | 2,048 → 2,560 | +25.00% |
| extension-properties | 23.658 → 32.333 | +36.67% | 27.053 → 36.088 | +33.40% | 3,584 → 10,752 | +200.00% |
| generic-extension-members | 29.048 → 40.436 | +39.20% | 33.626 → 45.168 | +34.33% | 4,608 → 12,288 | +166.67% |

The final ordinary-method medians are close. This is **not a speedup claim or a
stable budget pass**. The earlier paired candidate median was also approximately
11.4 ms, while the paired baseline changed from 9.795 to 11.420 ms between runs.
The observed movement cannot be attributed solely to the small scope-pruning
change. All earlier results, including the original +16.58% ordinary regression,
remain below.

| Workload | Median heapUsed delta before → after (bytes) | p95 heapUsed delta before → after (bytes) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ordinary-methods | 2,854,732 → 3,076,916 | 2,945,168 → 3,433,960 |
| extension-properties | 5,724,584 → 9,140,684 | 5,825,240 → 9,852,808 |
| generic-extension-members | 7,498,060 → 12,020,780 | 7,577,992 → 12,566,216 |

The memory metric is the signed difference in `heapUsed` immediately before and
after compilation. It includes any GC during compilation. It is neither an
allocation count nor per-compilation peak heap or peak RSS.

### Bounded ordinary-workload profiles

The original +16.58% paired ordinary regression triggered CPU profiling before
cost acceptance. Both clean graphs received 80 rotating ordinary warmups, followed
by 128 profiled compilations each at a 500 µs sampling interval. GC was requested
before each profile. These were short samples of the same 32-method source,
separate from benchmark timings.

| Profile observation | Baseline b19a56a7 | Candidate ed910584 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Captured samples | 957 | 1,054 |
| Inclusive reference emission samples | 158 / 16.51% | 247 / 23.43% |
| Inclusive NullableMetadataPlan samples | Absent | 11 / 1.04% |
| Inclusive common compiler-attribute definition writing | Absent | 25 / 2.37% |

Most added sampled work lies in metadata emission, including common fallback
attribute planning/writing and additional method/row emission. The nullable
planner does not account for the whole observed latency difference. Its empty
method scopes did cause avoidable map insertions and repeated context/attribute
passes, so that small correction was made and checked for metadata equivalence.
No isolated performance gain is inferred from the profile or the later paired run.

Profile provenance and hashes: [cpu-profile.json](cpu-profile.json).
Stack sample summary: [cpu-profile-summary.json](cpu-profile-summary.json).
The original profiles are retained losslessly as
[baseline.cpuprofile.gz](cpu-profiles/baseline.cpuprofile.gz) and
[candidate.cpuprofile.gz](cpu-profiles/candidate.cpuprofile.gz); decompress them to
inspect the original Chrome/V8 profile. Hashes in the provenance describe the
uncompressed files. Profile elapsed times are not benchmark samples.

### Exact ordinary-control size accounting

[ordinary-metadata.json](ordinary-metadata.json) records the complete control's
relevant rows and raw attributes, plus a genuine Roslyn build of the identical
source using the pinned .NET 10 toolchain.

| Metadata table | Baseline b19a56a7 | Candidate ed910584 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TypeRef | 1 | 5 |
| TypeDef | 2 | 4 |
| Field | 0 | 1 |
| MethodDef | 32 | 34 |
| Param | 32 | 33 |
| MemberRef | 0 | 2 |
| CustomAttribute | 0 | 6 |

The two added local definitions are internal sealed
`Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.EmbeddedAttribute` and
`System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RefSafetyRulesAttribute`. They add one
constructor each and the latter's public readonly `int Version` field and
constructor parameter. The six custom attributes are:

- `RefSafetyRulesAttribute(11)` on the module.
- `CompilerGeneratedAttribute` and `EmbeddedAttribute` on each local definition.
- `AttributeUsageAttribute(Module, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = false)` on
  `RefSafetyRulesAttribute`.

The actual Roslyn 5.3 build also emits the identical module attribute blob
`01 00 0b 00 00 00 00 00`. It references the existing public .NET target attribute;
the closed registry surface used by this benchmark requires local fallback
definitions. There are no extension grouping/marker types or nullable attributes
in this ordinary control. This is +512 bytes / +25% in the aligned PE, not an
extension declaration count effect.

### Implementation-author correctness-cost sign-off

After the byte-equivalence check, native consumer/reflection qualification,
profiles and paired comparisons, the implementation author and integration owner
accept the quantified whole-revision correctness cost. The final extension
property workload has median **+36.67%** and p95 **+33.40%**; the generic extension
workload has median **+39.20%** and p95 **+34.33%**. The original ordinary paired
**+16.58% median / +23.56% p95** remains part of the record; the later near-flat
ordinary result does not erase it or establish a stable performance gate.

All PE increases are also explicitly accepted: **ordinary +512 bytes / +25%;
extension properties +7,168 bytes / +200%; generic extension members +7,680 bytes /
+166.67%**. The ordinary C# 14 closed-reference contract is accounted for above.
Extension assemblies additionally contain discoverable grouping/marker types,
property semantics, and generic constraint/reference metadata that the baseline
did not emit. Those structures enable the independently compiled Roslyn clients
qualified by this batch. Aligned file increments amplify percentages in these
small PEs, so both percentages and byte increases are retained.

This is explicit author sign-off under CONTRIBUTING.md for a measured correctness
tradeoff, reviewed by the integration owner. It is not independent reviewer
approval, an isolated extension/hash overhead measurement, or a claim of a
speedup. The compared revisions include the complete metadata composition; none
of these costs is silently rebased into a passing threshold.

## Remaining acceptance

Keep #664 open for the separate source-binding/lowering acceptance still requiring
completion, including write-only extension property lookup, static generic methods
with their own type parameters in generic extension blocks, and extension compound
assignment operators. Export interoperability alone does not establish those
language behaviors. Additional runtime/backend acceptance and broader staged
qualification remain owned by their corresponding workstreams.
